steps.description: Design and execute a numerical experiment to test the hypothesis on "solution space rigidity" in small feedforward networks. Steps:

Conduct a targeted numerical experiment to test the concentration of measure hypothesis on solution space rigidity. Generate a smooth analytic target function (e.g., a high-degree polynomial or trigonometric combination), sample w constraint points (w ∈ {10, 20, 30, 50, 100}), train small feedforward networks (1-2 hidden layers, tanh activation) with widths N_h ∈ [4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128], and compute the minimal N_c(w) achieving ≤1e-3 absolute error on a held-out validation set of 100 independent points. Fix random seeds, use Adam with early stopping, and record training/validation MSE and N_c(w) trend.

We will test the algebraic dependency hypothesis by measuring the minimal hidden layer width N_c(w) that achieves zero violation (max absolute error ≤ 1e-3) on a held-out constraint set, as w (constraint sample count) varies. We will use a small 2-layer tanh MLP, scan N_h ∈ {4,8,16,32,64,128}, and evaluate N_c(w) trend. If N_c(w) saturates at a small finite value, we conclude rigidity; if no N_h ≤ 128 achieves the criterion, we conclude fatness. We will fix random seeds, use Adam with early stopping, and report training vs. held-out error curves.

plans.objective: [DIM: structure] The bootstrap solution space of small feedforward networks exhibits an algebraic dependency structure that remains low-dimensional (rank ≤ 3) even as w increases, causing N_c(w) to saturate at a finite value independent of w in the scanned range. | predict: N_c(w) ∈ {8, 16, 32} for all w ∈ {10, 20, 50, 100} (≤ 2× variation threshold). | pro: Directly tests the "rigidity via low-rank structure" hypothesis; aligns with concentration of measure and solvability of overconstrained systems; easy to verify via SVD or neural tangent kernel analysis. | con: May fail if the problem is inherently high-dimensional or if the network lacks sufficient capacity to exploit structural constraints; requires careful choice of basis functions.

steps.description: Implement a numerical experiment to test the rigidity hypothesis. Construct a small feedforward network (1-2 hidden layers, tanh activation) to approximate a target function (e.g., polynomial/trigonometric). For each w in {10, 20, 50, 100}, generate w random training samples and a large independent validation set (1000 points). For each hidden width N_h in [4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128], train the network with Adam optimizer and early stopping. Record the minimum N_h achieving max absolute error ≤ 1e-3 on the validation set (N_c(w)). Compare N_c(w) across w to verify saturation (rank ≤ 3 algebraic dependency). Use fixed random seeds for reproducibility.

We will train with Adam (lr=1e-3, early stopping on validation loss plateau 10 epochs) across widths $N_h \in [4,8,16,32,64,128]$, record minimal $N_h$ satisfying zero violation per $w$, and visualize error landscapes to detect overfitting.
